items.title: Mike Davis interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2024
items.q: You were horn-mates with Tim Ries is that correct?

ctx.x: Yeah. Hundred percent. And you know I mean the one — Nelson Riddle comes to mind — I mean such a great arranger. And you know he was a trombone player, not a particularly great trombone player, but he was a trombone player, typically playing in a big band section, probably playing third trombone. And the way he learned how to write was he would write on little pieces of — you know like a single stave — and just write out some voicings. And he would get done with a rehearsal and just ask the guys to stick around…
You were horn-mates with Tim Ries is that correct?

items.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022
items.q: it was my friends who live in New York who had played in the horn section with the Stones, Mike Davis on trombone, Kent Smith on trumpet, and Andy Snitzer

ctx.x: We might as well talk about the Stones a little bit as long as we’re here. When you got the call or whatever to join, was there any question of whether you would or not?

Well weirdly enough when I got the call it was my friends who live in New York who had played in the horn section with the Stones, Mike Davis on trombone, Kent Smith on trumpet, and Andy Snitzer, the saxophone player who left the Stones to go with Paul Simon. So he was leaving, they needed a guy who played sax, piano, organ, which I can do that stuff. So when Andy was leaving they got together and decided that a few of the musicians that they knew who could be best suited for that, and they called me. It was like…
Were there written horn parts for you?
